The presentation can include and is not limited to, macules, patches, papules, plaques, and nodules, which are purple/red.
When occurring on the lower extremities, Kaposi sarcoma has a more classic initial presentation of purples patches.
Lesions on the face and neck have a predilection for the nose, eyelids, ears, and oral mucosa, particularly the hard palate.
The type of Kaposi sarcoma most likely to present on the head and neck is the AIDS-associated type.
The endemic type of Kaposi sarcoma may present with lymphadenopathy of the neck with mucosal involvement.
Some clues to that point to Kaposi sarcoma are vessels that are slightly more irregular, while angiosarcomas display cellular atypia.[11]
Cutaneous angiosarcoma is difficult to diagnose clinically due to often having a benign appearance.
Clinically, they appear as violaceous nodules and plaques, bruise-like lesions, and may appear to be hemorrhagic macules and patches.
Patients may also present with lesions mimicking hematomas, rosacea, cellulitis, and angioedema.
A full review of systems must be performed in anyone with a vascular lesion, as positive fevers, night sweats, and weight loss may be a clue to malignancy.
